strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: training LLM reasoning without ground-truth labels while avoiding training collapse
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Qwen2.5/3, Llama) and diverse benchmarks (math, code, instruction-following, multi-task)
Clear demonstration of training stability improvements through validation curves and voting accuracy analysis at different problem difficulty levels
Strong empirical results on primary mathematical reasoning benchmarks with up to +6.8% improvement over GT reward baseline
Intuitive core idea with clear presentation; good use of figures to communicate effectiveness
Reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, paraphrasing prompt, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: reduces to applying GRPO to both original and paraphrased problems; paraphrase-based consistency is well-established; 'contrastive agreement' framing is misleading as it lacks true contrastive learning in representation space
Computational cost inadequately addressed: method requires 2× (or more) training data generation but no runtime/FLOPs analysis provided despite being significant practical barrier

Paraphrase quality and diversity critically under-explored: all paraphrases from single model (Qwen3-32B) with fixed prompt; no ablation on paraphrasing strategy or analysis of semantic equivalence; no sensitivity analysis to paraphrase quality

Claims of surpassing GT-labeled rewards lack rigorous validation: no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or controlled comparison; possible confounds from paraphrases providing implicit additional signal not available to GT baselines
Limited theoretical justification: unclear why dual-path cross-reference specifically prevents collapse versus simpler regularization approaches; no formal analysis of mechanism

Mixed results on non-mathematical tasks undermine generality claims: instruction-following (IFEval) sometimes worse than baselines; multi-task results often below GT reward; method appears primarily suited to mathematical reasoning, contradicting claims of general effectiveness
Reward hacking risk remains inadequately analyzed: acknowledged risk when prompts are 'excessively complex' but no systematic characterization of when/why this occurs; no failure case analysis
Incomplete sensitivity analysis: number of paraphrases (n=8) fixed with no ablation; limited hyperparameter exploration; missing comparisons to alternative consistency-based or ensemble methods
Statistical rigor lacking: no significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported for any results; some results appear identical (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B: 65.4% both GT and Co-Reward)
Test-time training results mixed: Table 2 shows inconsistent improvements, with baseline Majority-Voting sometimes competitive

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear illustrations of reward hacking behavior in self-rewarding methods; training collapse is a real and timely issue

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Llama), training sets (MATH, DAPO-14k, OpenRS), and diverse benchmarks; extensive ablations and stability analysis
Strong stability results with compelling evidence that Co-rewarding prevents collapse; Figures 3-6 effectively demonstrate improved training dynamics compared to baselines
Solid empirical results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks with consistent improvements (+3.31% average); notable 94.01% Pass@1 on GSM8K surpassing GT-Reward
Clear conceptual framework grounded in invariance beyond single-view supervision; intuitive philosophy that motivates the two-pronged approach
Comprehensive reproducibility efforts with detailed hyperparameters, promised code release, and implementation details in appendix
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Co-rewarding-I applies standard contrastive learning to paraphrases, and Co-rewarding-II uses established EMA-based teachers (BYOL/DINO). The contribution is combining existing techniques rather than proposing novel mechanisms

Critical dependency on question rephrasing quality: Co-rewarding-I collapses on DAPO-14k but not MATH, attributed to rephrasing quality without analysis; no sensitivity analysis or ablation on rephrasing strategy
Lack of theoretical justification: No formal analysis of why contrastive agreement prevents reward hacking or convergence guarantees; the invariance framing is intuitive but not rigorously justified
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices without justification: EMA schedule parameters (αstart=0.99 to αend=0.9999) appear unmotivated; no ablation studies on these critical parameters

Pseudo-label quality concerns: Initial pseudo-label accuracy ~0.25 (Figure 6); majority voting is crude strategy with no exploration of alternatives; circular dependency between teacher and policy updates
Mixed results across settings and domains: Minimal improvements on LiveCode/CRUX; Co-rewarding-II sometimes underperforms GT-Reward on MMLU-Pro; general capabilities (IFEval) show no clear advantage
No statistical rigor: Single runs without error bars or confidence intervals; some claimed improvements (e.g., +2.94% vs GT-Reward) could be within noise margins
Incomplete analysis: No computational overhead quantification; missing comparison of training time; speculative explanation for MATH vs DAPO-14k behavior; limited failure case analysis
Overstated claims about surpassing GT-Reward: Gains are often 2-3% across multiple settings; unclear if differences are statistically significant; MMLU-Pro shows mixed results
Limited generalization evidence: Strongest results only on mathematical reasoning; inconsistent improvements on code generation; no evidence this addresses collapse in other domains

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and analyzes training collapse in self-rewarding methods due to reward hacking under self-consistent illusion
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple LLM families, training sets, benchmarks, with extensive ablations and test-time training results
Strong empirical results: consistent improvements over baselines (+3-7%), reaches/surpasses GT-Reward in several cases, demonstrates stable training curves
Clear conceptual framework: elegant distinction between data-side (analogy-invariance) and model-side (temporal invariance) supervision with effective visualizations
Thorough mechanistic analysis: reward/response-length trade-offs, pseudo-label accuracy tracking, and illustrative case studies clearly demonstrate why baselines fail
Preserves general capabilities: demonstrates no catastrophic forgetting on MMLU-Pro and IFEval, supporting broad applicability
Detailed reproducibility support: complete hyperparameters, implementation details, promised code release
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Co-rewarding-I is straightforward application of question rephrasing; Co-rewarding-II applies standard EMA teacher updates from self-distillation; no new algorithmic principles
Lack of theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why contrastive agreement or EMA decoupling prevent collapse, missing convergence analysis and stability guarantees
Unexplained anomalous results: Co-rewarding surpassing GT-Reward (94.01% vs 87.26% on GSM8K) is surprising and deserves investigation; raises concerns about robustness
Co-rewarding-I generalization issues: stability depends on dataset (stable on MATH, collapses on DAPO-14k); requires expensive rephrasing; quality-impact relationship not analyzed
Missing computational cost analysis: no wall-clock time or FLOPs comparison for rephrasing and teacher maintenance; practical deployment implications unclear
Incomplete mechanistic understanding: unclear which factors drive stability (data diversity? contrastive filtering? computational overhead?); missing targeted ablations isolating components
Limited experimental scope: all experiments on mathematical reasoning; generalization to other RL domains (alignment, summarization) unexamined

Design choices under-justified: majority voting vs. alternatives not compared; EMA schedule sensitivity not ablated; rollout count impact not studied; different training steps for I vs II across methods
